Issued at 153 AM MDT Tue Oct 13 2026

What I have noticed this year is that when we get a certain kind of 
weather, is that it sticks around for a while, with a few exceptions 
of course. Examples include the several heat waves we had this year, 
the monsoon over the summer that seemed to drag on forever and the 
period in the latter part of June when we seemed to have a severe 
thunderstorm somewhere in the area. The past few weeks have been an 
example, we had a prolonged period of wet weather in the middle of 
September. We then had a strong ridge across the area for better 
part of three weeks, bringing dry and warm weather for most of the 
latter part of September as well as the first several days of 
October. We are now in the period of the everlasting moisture, 
courtesy of what was left of Tropical Storm Rachel and now a slow 
moving bowling ball, AKA and upper level low, now dropping 
southward over Nevada. And this system will influence our weather 
for a couple more days. 

For the third night in a row, we continue to have areas of showers 
moving across the area. Satellite imagery shows cloud tops are 
slowly warming, so coverage and intensity of showers should 
gradually decrease through the rest of the night, although some will 
linger through the night. As for today, it will be fairly similar to 
yesterday with another day of below normal temperatures and plenty 
of cloud cover. There will also be showers around through the day. 
However, with the low moving further way, coverage should be less 
than previous days. This is also the first day of the past few there 
is not an excessive rainfall outlook, so amounts should be less.

Steadier precipitation may increase tonight though, especially 
across southern and central Wyoming as the upper level low begins to 
make a turn to the east and moves across Colorado. This will turn 
flow to the east and bring some upslope flow into the area. The area 
looks to be on the northern edge of the deeper moisture though, so 
rainfall amounts do not look excessive at night. The most favored 
areas will be across the Wind River Basin to Casper with the upslope 
flow. I will discuss amounts later in the discussion. And this 
includes potential snowfall amounts in the mountains. Precipitation
will continue into Wednesday, but there is some uncertainty here.
There are some differences in guidance in regards to the
movement of the upper level low. The bottom line is, the 
further north it moves, the further to precipitation can wrap 
back into the area. The greatest confidence for rain will be 
from Natrona County southwest to Rock Springs and on to the 
south and east. Chances drop further north and west, with the 
northwestern part of Wyoming largely dry on this day. And this 
continues through Wednesday night as well as the low continues 
to move eastward.

There is one more concern for Wednesday night. As the upper level 
low moves eastward, lee cyclogenesis will occur over Colorado. This 
will tighten the pressure gradient across the area, increasing 
wind. Much of the area East of the Divide as well as southern 
Wyoming have a greater than 1 out of 2 chance of wind gusts past 30 
mph from later Wednesday night through Thursday. The strongest gust 
would be in the wind prone areas in Johnson County, where there is a 
1 in 3 chance of gusts past 50 mph. Low level winds do not look 
sufficient for high wind though. Following this, all rain ends on 
Thursday and then ridging builds back over the area, bringing 
a return to dry conditions and near to somewhat above normal 
temperatures.

PRECIPITATION AND SNOW AMOUNTS...We still start with precipitation. 
Reasoning remains similar to yesterday with the highest amounts in 
the mountain ranges and across central and southern Wyoming. Most of 
the mountains, except for the far north, as well as much of the Wind 
River Basin and Natrona County, have at least a 3 out of 5 chance of 
a quarter of an inch of precipitation or greater through Wednesday 
night. The 1 out of 2 chance of three quarters of an inch or greater 
runs roughly from east of Riverton to Casper and southward to the 
Continental Divide. The smallest amounts would be across northern 
Wyoming as the low digs to the south. 

Now on to snowfall. Snow levels look to bottom out Tuesday night 
into Wednesday, with 700 millibar temperatures falling to around 
7000 to 7500 feet. Most of the mountain ranges have at least a 1 in 
2 chance of an inch of snow from Tuesday morning through Wednesday 
night. However, for advisory level amounts, which is 6 inches or 
greater, the only location is the Wind River Range. Most areas above 
9000 feet continue to have at least a 1 in 2 chance of 6 inches of 
snow or more. The highest peaks will likely (a greater than 2 out of 
3 chance) see over a foot of additional snow, but impacts here are 
few to none. So, we will keep the advisory going for now. The
